title: Machine shop
content: Hadley’s basement machine shop was a patchwork of scavenged tech, old-world tools, and the raw hum of function over form. The space, carved into the bones of an abandoned industrial easement, was a maze of workbenches laden with half-dissembled machinery, oil-stained schematics, and cleaning rags stiff with metal dust. A pair of lathes lined one wall, their once-pristine surfaces dulled by years of makeshift repairs and relentless repurposing. Overhead, cables snaked like tangled roots, feeding power to dim monitors that flickered with blueprints and diagnostic scans. A circular saw rested beside a crate of salvaged alloys, its teeth still sharp from its last battle against stubborn scrap. Power tools—some decades old, some newer but equally abused—were scattered across surfaces, their cords looping around welding masks and grease-slicked wrenches. The air smelled of ozone, coolant, and the distinct bite of hot metal, all mixing with the ever-present damp of subterranean confinement. She had made this space her own, a private refuge where the outside world’s entropy could be unraveled one bolt at a time.
